title: Korea's Public Holiday Calendar: What Actually Closes (And How to Plan Around It)
html:
Planning a trip to Korea and wondering if your travel dates might land on a public holiday? You're asking the right question. Korea has a handful of holidays that barely change daily life for a visitor — and two "big" ones that can quietly wreck a poorly timed itinerary if you don't know about them. This guide breaks down what actually closes, what stays open (often a surprise), and how to plan around the calendar instead of getting caught out by it.

Gyeongbokgung Palace, one of Seoul's five royal palaces. Palaces like this one are usually fine to visit during holidays — they're actually one of the better places to be.

The two "everyone goes home" holidays: Seollal and Chuseok

Out of all of Korea's holidays, only two really matter for trip planning: Seollal (설날, Lunar New Year) and Chuseok (추석, a harvest festival often compared to Thanksgiving). Both are 3-day stretches where a huge share of the country travels to their hometown to see family — this mass movement is called gwiseong (귀성). Trains, highways, and domestic flights get genuinely packed for a few days around each one.

These aren't fixed calendar dates — they follow the lunar calendar, so they move every year. In 2026, Seollal fell in mid-February and Chuseok fell on September 24–26. Looking ahead, Seollal 2027 is expected around February 6–8 and Chuseok 2027 around September 14–16 — but double-check the exact dates closer to your trip, since lunar-to-solar conversions can shift by a day between sources.

💡 What locals actually do: Korean friends and coworkers often set an alarm for the exact minute train tickets go on sale — usually about a month before the holiday — because KTX (the high-speed train) seats for popular routes can sell out within minutes. If you're planning to travel between cities right around Seollal or Chuseok, book as early as the booking window allows, or consider staying inside one city during those few days instead.

What actually closes — and what surprisingly doesn't

Convenience stores like GS25, CU, and 7-Eleven are Korea's holiday safety net — most locations stay open every single day of the year, including Seollal and Chuseok.

Here's the part that trips up first-time visitors: the things you'd expect to close (banks, post offices, government offices) do close on every public holiday, not just the big two. But most of what travelers actually use — convenience stores, department stores, large shopping malls, and subway/bus service — keeps running close to normal hours.

The one exception is small, independently run places: family-owned restaurants, local noodle shops, and traditional market stalls. A lot of these close for part or all of the Seollal/Chuseok 3-day stretch because the owners are traveling too, especially outside Seoul. If you're relying on a specific small restaurant for a meal during one of these windows, it's worth checking their social media or calling ahead — don't assume it's open just because it was open yesterday.

Royal palaces (Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung, and Changgyeonggung) are actually a great choice during Seollal and Chuseok: the Korea Heritage Service typically waives admission for everyone during the holiday stretch and runs special guard-changing ceremonies, on top of the usual free entry for anyone wearing hanbok (traditional Korean clothing). Each palace is normally closed one fixed day a week though (Gyeongbokgung is closed on Tuesdays, for example) — that closure is unrelated to the holiday calendar, so check it separately.

The other holidays: mostly business as usual

Single-day holidays rarely change much for visitors — if anything, popular spots like this one get a little busier with local day-trippers.

Korea has quite a few other public holidays through the year — New Year's Day, Independence Movement Day, Children's Day, Buddha's Birthday, Memorial Day, Liberation Day, National Foundation Day, Hangeul Day, and Christmas. For a tourist, these are low-stress: banks and offices close, but attractions, restaurants, shops, and transit all run normally. The only thing to watch for is a 3-day weekend — when one of these single-day holidays lands next to a Saturday or Sunday, popular attractions, cafes, and highways can get noticeably more crowded with Korean domestic travelers, even though nothing is actually closed.

One quirk worth knowing: Korea has a rule called daeche gonghyuil (대체공휴일, "substitute holiday"). If a holiday falls on a weekend, the government usually hands back the next regular weekday as a day off instead. That's why some years have an extra random Monday off that doesn't appear on older calendars — if a date you're checking looks off, this is usually why.

Planning your trip around the calendar

None of this means you should avoid Korea's holiday season — a quieter, locals-focused atmosphere (and sometimes free palace entry) can actually be a nice time to visit, as long as you plan around the travel crunch.

The short version: you don't need to avoid Korea's holidays, you just need to plan around them. Book intercity trains and buses early if your trip overlaps with Seollal or Chuseok, have a backup restaurant in mind if you're set on a small local spot during those dates, and expect a bit more company at famous sights during 3-day weekends. Everything else — ATMs, convenience stores, subways, and most restaurants — works the same as any other day.

Holiday When Impact on travelers
New Year's Day January 1 Low — banks/offices closed, everything else normal
Seollal (Lunar New Year) 3-day stretch, ~early-mid February (moves yearly) High — book transport early, some small eateries closed
Independence Movement Day March 1 Low
Children's Day May 5 Low-medium — family attractions busier
Buddha's Birthday ~mid-late May (moves yearly) Low — temples hold lantern events, worth visiting
Memorial Day June 6 Low
Liberation Day August 15 Low
Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) 3-day stretch, ~mid-late September (moves yearly) High — book transport early, free palace entry
National Foundation Day October 3 Low
Hangeul Day October 9 Low
Christmas Day December 25 Low — cafes and shopping streets get festive and busy

meta_description: A first-timer's guide to Korea's public holidays: what closes, what stays open, and how to plan your trip around Seollal and Chuseok.
